00-problem: A criminal moves money through five banks. Each bank sees only its own piece. Each piece looks normal, so each alert is cleared. Problem one: alert fatigue. An estimated 85 to 95 percent of AML alerts are false positives. Problem two: blind spots. On IBM's public laundering data, the best placed bank holds 43.8 percent of a ring's accounts, and sees the whole ring in none of 36 rings. Problem three: proof. Reports are assembled by hand. Seen together, the ring is obvious. This is BankWeave.
01-landing: BankWeave is a team of AI agents that investigates money-laundering alerts across many banks, with FalkorDB as their shared brain.
02-explainer: Each bank lives in its own isolated FalkorDB graph and sees only itself. Salted, hashed account ids stitch them into a consortium graph, and only there does the ring appear. This bank sees 37.5 percent of it. PageRank finds the hub, and every scene here is a live FalkorDB query, with its Cypher.
03-dashboard: The console runs live on FalkorDB Cloud: open cases, alerts decided, which claims are independently supported, what waits for a human, and the engine's own health. The agents share a task blackboard stored in the graph.
04-alerts: Most alerts are innocent, and Triage clears them in milliseconds, with a reason. Here, FalkorDB's connected components show a two-account island at one bank: cleared, with the evidence attached.
05-ring: One bank sees fragments. The consortium sees one ring across four banks. In the graph explorer, one read-only Cypher query returns the whole ring that no bank graph contains, and PageRank shows where the money pools.
06-case: Each case has its own graph. Every claim links to evidence, and every piece of evidence keeps the Cypher that produced it, while a Skeptic agent argues the innocent side. AI agents overcount evidence: many paths, few real sources. BankWeave counts independent origins, not paths. And when a KYC fact changes, the change cascades to every claim and action that relied on it.
07-approval: Agents recommend; a human approves. A second model checks every report sentence against its evidence, and the audit dossier is sealed with a signed Merkle root.
08-hardware: The evidence starts at the card tap. This ESP32 terminal, running in Wokwi, posts a real tap over HTTPS to our live API, which approves it and writes a card transaction edge into FalkorDB Cloud. Here it is in the FalkorDB Browser: the Mumbai terminal and the cards that tapped it. EMVLab, an independent decoder, reads the chip data correctly. Approvals are security key signatures over the case's Merkle root, and the enclave that hashes identities quarantines itself if tampered with. Simulated devices, real cryptography.
09-mcp: Everything the agents know is also served over the Model Context Protocol. One line adds BankWeave to Claude: seventeen read-only tools on the live graph. Ask whether a claim is really proven: three paths, but one independent source, so BankWeave scores it 0.26, not 0.59. Every answer carries the exact Cypher it ran, and writes are refused.
10-browser: This is not a mock-up. Here is our FalkorDB Cloud instance, and FalkorDB's own browser connected to it. The cross-bank ring in under two milliseconds. PageRank in three and a half. Every report sentence cites a claim that rests on evidence. Vector search finds behaviour twins at five banks.
11-lab: The FalkorDB Lab runs seventeen engine features in one click: native algorithms, full-text, vector search, JavaScript UDFs, ACLs and query profiles.
12-eval: And it is measured against IBM's labels. Graph triage beats the rule baselines, 25 of 28 reports passed the provenance gate, and where we fell short, the page says so.
13-end: No bank can see a laundering ring alone. BankWeave can. Many banks, one ring, every claim proven.
